Outrage is a feeling of intense anger that comes with a strong sense that something is deeply wrong — morally wrong, unjust, or indecent. It is not ordinary anger. It is anger that burns with moral force. When you feel outrage, you are not just upset — you are also shocked, and you feel that something should never have happened. There is a sense of violation, as if a rule of basic decency or fairness has been broken.

Think of it this way: if someone cuts in front of you in a queue, you might feel annoyed or irritated. But if you watch a powerful person abuse a helpless child and face no punishment, what you feel is outrage — a much deeper, heavier emotion.
The Two Faces of the Word

"Outrage" works in two closely related ways as a noun:

1. The emotion itself — the feeling inside a person or a group of people.

"There was widespread outrage when the company dumped toxic waste into the river."

Here, outrage is the reaction — the burning anger and disbelief that people felt.

2. The act or event that causes that feeling — something so offensive, cruel, or unjust that it deserves to be called an outrage.

"The unprovoked attack on civilians was an outrage."

Here, the act itself is being called an outrage — meaning it is a shocking violation of what is right and acceptable.

So the word can name the fire (the feeling) or the thing that lit the fire (the event). Context will always make it clear which one is meant.

Anger is a broad word. You can be angry about almost anything — a cold cup of coffee, a missed bus, a rude comment. Anger doesn't always carry a moral message.

Outrage is different. It almost always involves a sense of injustice or moral violation. It says: "This is not just bad for me personally — this is fundamentally wrong. This should not exist in a decent world."

This is why outrage often feels righteous — like you are angry on behalf of what is right, not just on behalf of yourself. A person can feel outrage about something that doesn't even affect them personally, simply because they see it as deeply unjust.

Outrage is also tied to shock and disbelief. When something outrages you, part of the feeling is: "How could this even happen? How dare they?" It carries an element of being stunned — as if your expectations of basic human decency have been violently betrayed.

This is why outrage tends to feel more explosive and urgent than regular anger. Regular anger can simmer quietly. Outrage tends to demand to be expressed.

Outrage is one of the most social of emotions. While a single person can feel outrage alone, the word is very often used to describe a shared reaction — an emotion felt by many people together.

"The verdict sparked public outrage across the country."
"His remarks caused outrage on social media."

When outrage spreads through a group — a community, a nation, the internet — it can become a powerful social force that drives protests, demands for justice, or political change. This is why you often see it paired with words like public outrage, mass outrage, or widespread outrage.

It is worth knowing that outrage is not always genuine. In modern usage, especially in the context of news and social media, people sometimes talk about manufactured outrage or performative outrage — situations where someone acts outraged not because they truly feel it, but because it is socially or politically useful for them to appear that way.

This distinction matters because the word is sometimes used critically:

"The politician's outrage over the issue felt hollow — he had ignored it for years."

So "outrage" can describe both authentic moral feeling and its hollow imitation.

• A sense of outrage — a feeling of outrage, often personal and deep.
  • Moral outrage — outrage specifically rooted in ethics or values.
  • Public outrage — outrage shared by many people in a society.
  • Express outrage / feel outrage — to show or experience the emotion.
  • Spark outrage / trigger outrage / cause outrage — to be the reason people feel outraged.
  • Outrage over something — outrage directed at a specific cause.

Outrage (noun) is a strong, shock-charged anger rooted in the feeling that something deeply unjust or indecent has occurred — it can refer to the emotion felt by a person or group, or to the terrible act that provoked that emotion.
